records.name: Tlaxcala
records.current_summary:
Tlaxcala is not among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count (22 of 32 states have legislated one).

No Tlaxcala-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; Mexico's national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: HRW's March 2025 state-by-state rundown of legal gender recognition records that Tlaxcala's congress passed a 2019 reform to the state Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, linking the decree text on the state congress's own site. The feature contrasts Tlaxcala with states it lists as still having no procedure, such as Tabasco and Tamaulipas. For this record it states the concrete legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update documents in Tlaxcala: an administrative route requiring no court proceeding.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national framework page Tlaxcala stands under: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2022 (the final states completed legalisation that year), federal protection against sexual-orientation discrimination since 2003, and — after the Supreme Court's 17 October 2018 ruling — a transgender person can change name and gender marker through a simple administrative procedure based on self-declaration, the page listing administrative legal gender recognition as available in Mexico City and 18 states. The page names Tlaxcala directly: its civil-union law took effect on 12 January 2017. It also notes outed LGBTQ soldiers face severe harassment and are often discharged; a visitor's practical exposure is the national baseline locally enforced.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national framework page names Yucatán directly: on 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners were able to marry and on 8 August 2013 the first same-sex couple legally married in the state; the Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022, and Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, still in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and elsewhere. The page also records the federal framework: same-sex acts decriminalised since 1871, tolerance of sexual diversity documented among Yucatán Maya groups, and the conversion-therapy ban passed federally by the Chamber of Deputies in March 2023 (267-104) after a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: HRW's state-by-state rundown of legal gender recognition (March 2025) carries a dedicated Yucatán entry: 'In 2024, the state's congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition', linking to the state's official gazette (Diario Oficial, 26 April 2024, on yucatan.gob.mx). This places Yucatán among the Mexican states with an administrative - rather than court-ordered - route for transgender people to update legal gender, which is the concrete local procedure a trans visitor's document situation turns on; the same feature explains which states lack any procedure.

sources.title: Diputados aprueban reforma en beneficio de la comunidad trans (La Jornada Zacatecas)
sources.claim: La Jornada Zacatecas, 23 December 2022, reports that with 14 votes in favour and 7 against, deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved the reform of the Family Code of the State of Zacatecas on gender identity, establishing the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community; the Justice Committee had already issued a positive opinion (dictamen) on the reform. This is the local record of the 2022 enactment against which this record's central claim — that Zacatecas is not among the states lacking a legislated gender-recognition procedure — is checked. Page verified via the Wayback Machine snapshot of 7 October 2025; the live ljz.mx URL is Cloudflare-blocked (HTTP 403).

sources.title: ¡Eso! Zacatecas prohíbe las terapias de conversión o los ECOSIG (Sopitas)
sources.claim: Sopitas, 30 August 2021, reports that on 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved prohibiting and sanctioning conversion therapies or 'ECOSIG' (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género) by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code — penalised with one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work against anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or promotes such practices; the same session also typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code. The article further records that the gender-identity law initiative debated alongside (constitutional and family-code reform) failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending at the time — the reform only passed in December 2022. Documents the protective state-level criminal-law floor applying in Zacatecas, with an explicit ban on practices aimed at changing gender identity.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State (Human Rights Watch)
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature on legal gender recognition carries a dedicated Zacatecas entry: in 2022 the state congress passed a reform amending the Family Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the law, both linked to the official state gazette (periodico.zacatecas.gob.mx). This is the per-state framework source consistent with the record's statement that, in HRW's March 2025 count (22 of 32 states having legislated a procedure at the time), Zacatecas is not among the states lacking one.

records.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
records.current_summary: No province-specific trans law, enforcement pattern or official statement was found: criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly, and the province has no facility or expression rule differing from the national position. Police-reported hate crime across all motivations is the lowest in the country alongside Manitoba (5.3 per 100,000 in 2024); a +51% rise that year was from very small absolute numbers. Risk assessed at parity with the national picture.
records.current_outOfScope: The province's low overall hate-crime rate and its 2024 percentage rise cover all motivations (race, religion, sexual orientation) from tiny absolute counts; neither is a trans-specific signal.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023, after a +34% jump in 2023); national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000 (with Manitoba), while Ontario recorded the highest (16.0); the province's +51% rise reflects only 19 incidents in 2023 to 29 in 2024 — very small absolute numbers, so the rate change is statistically fragile. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents.

sources.title: Changes to Vital Statistics Act Would Allow for Change of Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.claim: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 17 June 2021: proposed changes to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 would allow residents of the province who were not born there — but have lived there at least three months — to change their sex designation; the change certificate carries a $25 fee, counts as official provincial identification and 'could be leveraged by the applicant to update records in other jurisdictions,' serving as the identification document for people born outside the country. The release states the amendments align with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading that day and Royal Assent on 23 June 2021. Gives the province a resident-based legal gender-change route (three-month residency) relevant to document enrolment for trans people in Newfoundland and Labrador.

sources.title: Legislative Amendment Respects Rights of Transgender Individuals (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.claim: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 12 April 2016: an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 removes the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission (the December 2015 ruling on complaints from two trans women) and with LGBTQ advocates' requests. The province's gender-marker change on provincial records has therefore operated without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment (Royal Assent 13 April 2016).

sources.title: Changing Your Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador)
sources.claim: Current official Government of Newfoundland and Labrador page: applicants for a change of sex designation must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s (with consent of the other parent/guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15), and must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months; there is no fee for the change application, with charges applying only to official copies of updated documents (new birth certificate $35, or $30 online). The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate with an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the documented cross-border document caveat relevant to carrying provincial records elsewhere.

sources.title: P.E.I. transgender community applauds ID changes (CBC News)
sources.claim: CBC News, 18 April 2016, reports that the MacLauchlan government tabled a bill to amend the Vital Statistics Act so Islanders can change their gender on official documents by declaring the gender they identify with plus a letter from a doctor, with sex-reassignment surgery no longer required; Pride P.E.I. board member Jesse Macmillan welcomed the move, noting surgery is expensive and the closest provider was in Montreal, and called for a future third gender category, adding that many of his friends in Charlottetown identify outside the binary; a linked item on the article page reports Health PEI would cover the costs of three surgeries for transgender patients. PEI's gender-marker change on provincial documents has worked without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment.

sources.title: Improving diversity and inclusion on driver's licences (Government of Prince Edward Island news release)
sources.claim: Government of Prince Edward Island news release, 30 November 2018: Islanders may now select 'gender not listed' (shown on the licence as X) or 'prefer not to say' (blank) alongside male and female when identifying gender on a driver's licence; the release states PEI is the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say'/blank option, quoting Transportation, Infrastructure and Energy Minister Paula Biggar and PEERS Alliance. The change took effect 4 December 2018 at Access PEI locations, meaning provincial photo ID can carry an X or blank gender marker.

sources.title: Change of Gender Designation (Government of Prince Edward Island)
sources.claim: Official Government of PEI information page (content as captured in the Wayback Machine snapshot of 1 July 2022; the live page is bot-gated): an adult may apply for a change of gender designation if born in PEI and resident in the province for at least three months and not in the lawful custody of another person; a legal custodian may apply for a minor under 18 who was born on PEI and has lived in the province at least three months, with written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if aged 12 or older. The application requires completed forms including a physician statement, a written statement by the applicant, and signature arranged before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics — a provincial gender-marker regime operating without a surgery requirement and with physician attestation.

sources.title: N.S. transgender prisoner looking to challenge decision to hold her in men's prison - Saltwire / The Chronicle Herald
sources.claim: The Chronicle Herald reports (18 March 2025) that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence; the judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. This is the documented Nova Scotia case showing how a trans woman's correctional placement is being challenged and judicially reviewed in the province's custodial system.

sources.title: Grants to Support 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Groups, Provincial Conference - Government of Nova Scotia
sources.claim: The Government of Nova Scotia announced (10 June 2026) more than $176,000 through the first round of its new 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, with awards including $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth and $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, plus $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference; per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year. This is official, dated evidence of provincial funding and institutional support for 2SLGBTQIA+ communities across Nova Scotia.

sources.title: Province Releases First 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan - Government of Nova Scotia
sources.claim: The Government of Nova Scotia released (8 January 2026) the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022 - described as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people - and informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations; the plan maps actions to improve programs and policies and support full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people. This is official confirmation that Nova Scotia operates an explicit provincial inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation.

records.name: Quebec
records.current_summary:
Quebec's recorded profile rests on the national data series: Statistics Canada's March 2026 release on police-reported hate crime (2024 data) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally for a fourth consecutive year — +8% to 139, nearly triple 2020 — and identifies no trans-specific provincial pattern for Quebec.

No Quebec-specific anti-trans legislation, ordinance or incident series appears in the surviving sources, alongside national NGO analysis of the same police data; the province's largest city anchors one of the country's most established organised 2SLGBTQ+ communities.

No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in the release windows, so it supports the record's national-parity assessment. sources.title: Quebec's new trans inmate policy goes against human rights, advocates say - CBC News
sources.claim: CBC News reports (19 June 2025) that Quebec's public security minister announced transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison; advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is dated, province-specific evidence of an official Quebec policy change reversing the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

sources.title: Gender Identity Protected by the Quebec Charter of Rights - Éducaloi
sources.claim: Éducaloi reports that on 10 June 2024 Quebec's Human Rights Tribunal found a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training; the page notes gender identity and expression were added as prohibited grounds of discrimination under Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms in 2016, and cites 2021 census data that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older (0.27% of those aged 15-34) identify as transgender. This is Quebec-specific enforcement evidence that trans people can win discrimination claims under provincial law.

sources.title: Center for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec - IMK
sources.claim: IMK's case note on Centre for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec records that after a two-month trial with 29 witnesses the Quebec Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people, that the Court of Appeal largely upheld the decision (2024 QCCA 348), and that the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. It is a dated, lawyer-verified account of the landmark Quebec court outcome that reshaped the province's rules on sex designation and identity documents.

records.name: Ontario
records.current_summary:
No province-specific anti-trans statute, policy or official hostility is on record: while two other provinces have legislated restrictions on trans names, pronouns or care, Ontario's government has not.

Criminal law and human-rights protection operate federally and uniformly. The national police-reported hate-crime series (Statistics Canada, March 2026) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally — +8% to 139 in 2024, a fourth consecutive increase — without identifying a trans-specific provincial pattern for Ontario.
records.current_outOfScope: Ontario's top provincial hate-crime rate covers all motivations (race/ethnicity, religion and sexual orientation dominate) and is not a trans-specific measure; it should not be read as gender-identity risk by itself.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023), national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, above the national figure — the only province-specific number in this release pointing above the national average. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting is influenced by awareness and community trust.

sources.title: 'Parents must be fully involved' in student's decision to change pronouns, Ontario education minister says - CTV News
sources.claim: CTV News reports (28 August 2023) that Ontario's education minister, Stephen Lecce, said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronouns at school, speaking the same week Saskatchewan joined New Brunswick in legislating parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names and pronouns; Lecce added that teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child, and Ontario did not adopt such legislation at that time. The article documents the Ontario government's stance on pronoun and name rules in schools at the peak of the 2023 Canadian pronoun-policy wave - the province held the line against legislating parental consent.

sources.title: Policy on preventing discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression - Ontario Human Rights Commission
sources.claim: The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations; it defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.
